title: The strawberry
hookLine: chased by a tiger, hanging from a vine over another tiger, a man tastes a wild strawberry (Buddhist parable, as retold in Zen)

cards: A man is walking across a field when he hears it: a growl. A tiger, coming fast. He runs.
He reaches the edge of a cliff, grabs the root of a wild vine, and swings himself over the edge. For a moment he's safe. He hangs there, breathing hard.
The tiger paces above him, sniffing. He looks down. Far below, a second tiger is waiting for him to fall.
And then two mice, one white and one black, come out and begin, little by little, to gnaw through the vine.

teach.b: Then he sees it. Growing out of the cliff face, just within reach: a wild strawberry, red and ripe. Holding the vine with one hand, he picks it with the other.
And the story ends: how sweet it tasted! That's the Zen telling, and it stops right there, on the sweetness, without rescuing him. The story has older roots.
An Indian parable tells of a man hanging in a well over a monster, with honey dripping into his mouth.
It appears in Buddhist writings, in the Hindu epic the Mahabharata, and it traveled west too, into the medieval Christian legend of Barlaam and Josaphat.
The older tellings read it as a warning: the mice are day and night, eating through a life's time, and the honey is the pleasure that distracts from the danger.
The Zen retelling turns it around. The tigers are still there. The mice still gnaw.
Nothing is fixed. But in the middle of all that, there is a strawberry, and he tastes it completely. Not in spite of the danger, and not by ignoring it.
Right there, knowing. Everyone is on the vine.
Nobody gets off the cliff. You could spend the whole time staring up at one tiger and down at the other, or notice what's growing right in front of you. Look back at this whole week.
The cup, emptied. The woman, set down at the river.
Is that so. The moon that stays. The bowl, washed.
The finger and the moon. And now, one strawberry. Seven Zen stories, each pointing at the same place: right here.

how: Zen teachers retell the strawberry parable to point at full attention in the present moment, and some meditation teachers use mindful eating, tasting one small thing slowly, as a practice.

o: a reward that comes after you escape danger
tasting what's sweet right now, even on the vine
a fruit offered at a Zen temple altar

p: day and night, in older readings

games.q: you're hanging from a vine: one tiger above, one below, two mice gnawing. a ripe strawberry grows within reach. what do you do?
o: pick the strawberry and taste it.
games.why: he picks it with his free hand. how sweet it tasted! the Zen telling ends there, without rescuing him.

practice: If you have something to eat or drink nearby, a berry, a sip of tea, a piece of bread, take it slowly; if not, remember the last thing you really tasted. Notice the first taste, then how it changes: the texture, the temperature.
Let your worries hang on the vine for a moment, and just taste.

wordCard.voice: The strawberry. Between two tigers, on a vine the mice are gnawing, a man picks a wild strawberry and tastes it fully.

carryVoice: Your line: how sweet it tasted. Seven Zen stories, and that's the week.
